chapter_theme: The emptiness of being unlearned: the unlearned person's speech, native wit, looks, wealth and rank all fail to count. The chapter is the harshest in the book on this point, and its contempt is largely about assemblies and public standing.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the unlearned have no right to speak in assembly (401-403), the fault of their native understanding (404-405), then their uselessness, looks, wealth and rank (406-409), and their failure to attain the human (410).

401.reading: Holding forth in an assembly without complete learning is like playing a board game with no marked board.
401.nuance: The image is exact: a game without a board isn't a bad game, because no move can mean anything. The fault is the absence of a shared frame, not lack of cleverness.

402.reading: For the unlearned to set their heart on speech is like desiring womanhood, or a woman, in one who lacks both breasts.
402.nuance: A crude comparison that rests on a narrow view of women's bodies. It is one of the verses where the book's period shows, and it shouldn't be softened. The commentators disagree on who is desiring.

positions.position: The unlearned man himself longs to speak, and this is like such a woman longing for womanhood: it gets nowhere, or brings laughter.
positions.quote: கல்வியில்லாதவன் ஒருவன் அவையின்கண் ஒன்று சொல்லுதலை அவாவுதல்

positions.position: The fault lies with the listener who wants to hear the unlearned, and this is like being infatuated with such a woman.

403.reading: Even the unlearned are very good, if only they can stay silent before the learned.
403.nuance: Dry praise. Parimelazhagar takes பெறின் seriously: it marks the condition as hard to meet, since those who don't know themselves can't manage it. The verse's sting is that knowing when to be silent would itself take the knowledge they lack.

404.reading: However excellent an unlearned person's brightness may be, the wise do not accept it.
404.nuance: The verse grants the brightness and refuses it recognition, so this is a claim about what the wise will credit and not about what the person has.

positions.position: It isn't real understanding: any good result is a chance hit, like letters traced by accident.
The natural intelligence may be real. The wise simply won't accept him as distinguished in learning.

405.reading: An unlearned person's standing wilts once he meets and speaks.
405.nuance: The verse doesn't say with whom; the commentators supply a learned person. தகைமை is taken three ways: Parimelazhagar as his self-estimate, Manakkudavar as real greatness, and Kalaignar as a false pose. The first and third make the loss self-delusion ending, while the second makes it a real loss.

406.reading: The unlearned can only be said to exist; beyond that they are like barren saline land that yields nothing.
406.nuance: உளர் என்னும் மாத்திரையர் reduces a person to the bare fact of being said to exist. Kalaignar's walking corpses is stronger than the verse's image, which is about yield.

407.reading: The fine looks of one without subtle, penetrating understanding are like those of a well-made clay doll.
407.nuance: Parimelazhagar concedes that a fine body is itself a rare fruit of birth, which makes the point less a scorn of beauty than a statement that it needs learning to be worth anything.

408.reading: Wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good.
408.nuance: The verse says நல்லார், the good, and opposes it to கல்லார், the unlearned. The pairing makes the learned and the good one group by sound and by implication. Parimelazhagar glosses நல்லார் as கற்றார் outright.

positions.position: Wealth ruins the unlearned owner, while poverty doesn't ruin the good. That is why it is more painful.
positions.quote: திருகல்லாரைக் கெடுக்க, வறுமை நல்லாரைக் கெடாது நிற்றலான்

positions.position: The harm falls on others: given wealth, the unlearned make other people suffer.

409.reading: Though born high, the unlearned do not have the worth of those who are learned though born low.
409.nuance: The verse overturns the ranking but keeps the words மேல் and கீழ், so birth rank remains as something to be overturned. The argument is not that the distinction is false, only that learning outweighs it.

positions.position: Caste rank ends with the body while learning goes with the soul, so learning is superior. Caste rank itself is assumed.
positions.quote: உடலோடு ஒழியும் சாதி உயர்ச்சியினும், உயிரோடு செல்லும் கல்வி உயர்ச்சி சிறப்புடைத்து

positions.position: The honour of learning removes the distinction of high and low altogether.

410.reading: As beasts stand to people, so do others stand to those who have studied the shining books.
410.nuance: The chapter ends by removing the unlearned from the human as such. Parimelazhagar's logic is that the surplus of awareness which marks humans over animals is found in the learned, so the two aren't of one birth.

links.note: 404 denies that native brightness counts without learning; 373 says a person's own understanding prevails over any amount of study. On one reading, the Kural both dismisses innate understanding and calls it unbeatable.
Both treat wealth as worse for being held by the wrong person, but 1000 faults character and 408 faults learning. 1000's spoilt milk also shows the damage to the good thing, not only to others.

409 uses high and low birth as a working scale, even to overturn it. 972 denies the scale at the root: birth is the same for all beings, and only deeds differ. The two arguments against birth rank are different in kind.
After a chapter that places the unlearned among beasts, 414 opens a door: though you haven't studied, listen. The next chapter quietly withdraws the finality of this one.

source_issues: 407: Parimelazhagar's gloss reads சுவையான் where the verse has மண்; the sense suggests சுதையான் (of plaster), so this is probably a corruption.
404: Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் reads நிலைபெற்ற தூல் அறிவுடையார், probably a corruption of நூல்.
